desc: Project Blue Book ran from March 1952 to 17 December 1969 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and is the public face of the legacy era. Its own final accounting is 12,618 sightings recorded, of which 701 were never identified — a residue of 5.6 per cent that the Air Force has never explained and that no subsequent official study has revisited. Blue Book had five directors: Edward Ruppelt, Charles Hardin, George Gregory, Robert Friend and Hector Quintanilla. Its analytical output was governed from 1953-1954 onward by AFR 200-2 and JANAP 146, which between them restricted what could be said publicly about unexplained cases and routed operationally significant reports away from Blue Book entirely. That last point is not inference: the Bolender memorandum of 20 October 1969, recommending termination, states that UFO reports which could affect national security are made under JANAP 146 or AFM 55-11 and are not part of the Blue Book system. Blue Book was therefore, by the admission of the general who closed it, the disposal channel rather than the collection channel. The records — roughly 37 cubic feet of case files plus administrative files and Office of Special Investigations material — are at the National Archives on 94 rolls of microfilm (T-1206), and NARA states it has been unable to locate any documentation among them discussing the 1947 Roswell incident.

claims.text: The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender states that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system."
The same document states: "There is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function (Atch 8)."

The same document notes that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs were not a direct physical threat, and that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system" for a further sixteen years.
Paragraph 8 of the same document recommends that Blue Book records be transferred to an archive "for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts."

Paragraph 9 records Air University's conditions for accepting the records: that SAFOI answer all Blue Book queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained."

The same paragraph states SAFOI's view that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because Washington-area availability "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts."

Blue Book was staffed full-time by two officers, one NCO and one civilian, with Dr. J. Allen Hynek as scientific consultant until 1 July 1969; reporting procedures were defined in Air Force Regulation 80-17.

Department of Defense release No. 1077-69, 17 December 1969, announced termination, quoting Secretary Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," and stated that Blue Book records would be retired to the USAF Archives at Maxwell AFB with requests handled by SAFOI.

The National Archives states that Blue Book textual records are available for research "excluding names of people involved in the sightings," and comprise approximately 2 cubic feet of project/administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files and 3 cubic feet of AFOSI-related records, accessed via 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm (T-1206).
The National Archives states: "The National Archives has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico."
GAO reviewed Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at National Archives II and reported it "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947."

The January 1985 USAF fact sheet distributed by Wright-Patterson AFB, reproduced by the National Archives, records 12,618 sightings from 1947 to 1969 of which 701 remain "Unidentified," and states "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base."

The Bolender document carried sixteen attachments listed on a separate page; NICAP's published notes state that researcher Robert Todd spent years seeking their release and that several remain unidentified or unreleased.

dossier.denialPosture: The Air Force's position has been fixed since 17 December 1969 and restated verbatim for decades: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, none represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and none indicated extraterrestrial vehicles (DoD release No. 1077-69). The January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet adds the installation-specific denial that there are not now and never have been "any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base." Both are dated, attributable and institutional, and both are silent on the JANAP 146 and AFM 55-11 channel the Air Force's own termination paperwork describes.
dossier.narrative:
Project Blue Book is the most examined document set in the history of the subject and the least useful, and both facts follow from the same cause: it was never the file where the answer would be.

The Air Force ran three named UFO efforts in sequence. Project SIGN began in 1948, Project GRUDGE followed in 1949, and Blue Book was stood up in March 1952 under Air Force Regulation 80-17, which required base commanders to provide a UFO investigative capability and Air Force Systems Command to continue the project. The Bolender document of 20 October 1969 describes the resulting establishment with some precision: "Project Blue Book has two officers, one NCO and one civilian assigned on a full-time basis," plus Dr. J. Allen Hynek as a scientific consultant until 1 July 1969. Four people, one part-time academic, and a stated mission to determine whether UFOs threatened national security and whether they exhibited advanced technology. For seventeen years this was the entire visible federal apparatus.

The Bolender document is the load-bearing artifact. It was written as the staff package recommending termination, was released to researcher Robert Todd in January 1979, and reads as an internal cost-benefit memorandum rather than a scientific finding. Paragraph 4 contains the sentence that reorganises everything around it: after noting that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs posed no direct physical threat, the document observes that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system," then states that national-security-relevant reports move under JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11 "and are not part of the Blue Book system." JANAP 146 is the joint communications instruction governing CIRVIS reporting of vital intelligence sightings; AFM 55-11 governs operational reporting. Neither corpus has ever been assembled, declassified or transferred as a body. Whatever came up those channels between 1952 and 1969 is not in T-1206 and never was.

The same document then explains, in operational terms, why Blue Book was kept alive after its own premise was disclaimed. Paragraph 8 recommends that if Blue Book is terminated the records "should be transferred to an appropriate archive and preserved for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts." The reason given for preservation is reputational management, stated openly. Paragraph 9 goes further. Because witnesses had been promised confidentiality, "access to these records and the publications must be carefully reviewed and controlled," and the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information judged that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because ready availability in Washington "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts." Air University agreed to take the files on three conditions: that SAFOI answer all queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained." The Air Force decided, in writing, where to put the archive on the basis of how hard it would be for the public to reach.

The public announcement two months later, Department of Defense release No. 1077-69 of 17 December 1969, carries none of that. It quotes Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," cites the Condon report and the National Academy of Sciences review, and closes with the three conclusions that have been repeated ever since: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, no "unidentified" case represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and no "unidentified" case indicated extraterrestrial vehicles. Read against Bolender, the first conclusion is a statement about a filing system rather than about the sky, because the reports that could affect national security were routed elsewhere by regulation.

Custody is the second reason Blue Book is on this map. The National Archives holds approximately 2 cubic feet of project and administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files arranged chronologically, and 3 cubic feet of records relating to the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, arranged by OSI district and overseas command. NARA states that the textual records are available "excluding names of people involved in the sightings." The public Blue Book is therefore a redacted copy of the Air Force's own Blue Book, and the confidentiality rationale from Bolender paragraph 9 is the reason. NARA also states flatly that it "has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico." The General Accounting Office found the same when it reviewed Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at Archives II during its 1994-95 Roswell audit: the analysis of sightings from 1946 to 1953 "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947." The single most famous American recovery event does not appear in the official American UFO file. That is either evidence the event did not happen or evidence the file was not where such events were recorded, and Bolender tells you which architecture the Air Force actually built.

What the record does not show is equally specific. The Bolender document carries sixteen attachments listed on a separate page. Several are known and were released separately; several have never surfaced. There is no public inventory of JANAP 146 CIRVIS traffic. There is no public accounting of the OSI material beyond the three cubic feet NARA holds. And the January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet that NARA reproduces contains the categorical sentence "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base" - a dated, attributable, institutional denial about a specific installation, which is exactly the kind of statement this board catalogues rather than weighs.
openQuestions: No inventory, index or transfer of the JANAP 146 (CIRVIS) and AFM 55-11 UFO reporting corpus for 1952-1969 has ever been made public. Where does that traffic physically reside?

Several of the sixteen attachments to the 20 October 1969 Bolender staff package have never been released. What is in Atch 8, cited for the claim that Blue Book served no intelligence function, and Atch 10, cited for the JANAP 146 routing?
Does an unredacted Blue Book master copy containing witness names still exist in Air Force custody, and under what disposition authority?
The exact date, transfer authority and accession record for the movement of the files from Wright-Patterson to the USAF Archives at Maxwell and then to NARA is not stated on NARA's own page.
The text and successive amendments of AFR 200-2 (1953) and its provisions on public release of unidentified cases were not verified in primary form for this dossier and remain a research target.
Whether AFOSI retained a parallel UFO case series beyond the three cubic feet at NARA, and whether any of it was destroyed.
dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force's public-facing unidentified flying object investigation, headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and running from March 1952 until Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans, Jr. announced its termination on 17 December 1969. It succeeded Projects SIGN and GRUDGE and logged 12,618 sightings, of which 701 were closed as "Unidentified." Its textual records were retired to the USAF Archives and subsequently to the National Archives, where they are open as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, publication T-1206, within Record Group 341.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Air Force's own termination paperwork states in plain language that Blue Book was not the channel through which serious UAP reporting flowed. The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender records that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system," and in the same paragraph that "there is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function." That is a signed admission of a two-channel architecture: a public channel with a press office and a phone number, and a separate operational reporting channel whose corpus has never been inventoried, indexed or transferred to any archive. The same document shows the Air Force weighing where to store the Blue Book files specifically to manage researcher access, with the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information agreeing to "rigidly limit the right of access" and to "screen researcher's notes." Blue Book therefore sits on this board twice: as the mechanism that absorbed and normalised public interest for seventeen years, and as a custody object whose public copy was deliberately shaped before release.
